gotamaka.notes: All six listed suttas name the shrine near Vesālī. The entry describes an ascetic group. AN 5.294–302:1.1 includes gotamako in its list of ascetics. That form has its own DPD sense, gotamaka 2, omitted from the packet. The other three AN citation targets belong to preceding texts.

govinda.notes: DN 19:29.2–6 identifies the entry’s subject as Disampati’s priest and Jotipāla’s father. His son inherits the office and both titles, Govinda and Mahāgovinda, at DN 19:31.1–6. AN 6.54:21.1 explicitly calls the son Jotipāla Govinda. DN 23:35.3 lists the discourse title.

gundāvana.notes: Mahākaccāna stays in this grove at Madhurā in AN 2.38 and MN 84. The adjacent MN 83 opens in Maghadeva’s mango grove at Mithilā.

haliddavasana.notes: MN 57 and SN 46.54 both name the Koliyan town. Check the entry’s claim about another Buddha. In SN 46.54 the monks tell the Buddha about their conversation with wanderers. MN 56 is set at Nāḷandā and SN 46.53 at Sāvatthī.

hatthaka.notes: One biography covers both senses. AN 1.251 names the lay disciple of Āḷavī. In AN 3.127 the god manifests a solid body and recalls teaching as a human. Both episodes are in the entry. The deity’s DPD reference is numbered AN 3.127 here. AN 3.128 is set at Isipatana. Of the packet’s page matches, the relevant passages are AN 1.251, 2.132, 3.35, 3.127, 8.23–24 and SN 17.23. The recaps at AN 3.40:8.2 and AN 8.30:26.1 also list the Hatthaka discourses.

hatthigāma.notes: AN 8.22 and SN 35.125 place Elephant Village in Vajji territory. AN 8.21 and SN 35.124 concern the householder at Vesālī. DN 16:4.5.2 names the village on the Buddha’s itinerary.

hatthipāla.notes: The entry’s second AN reference also reaches the list of ancient teachers at AN 7.73:2.4. In AN 6.54 the English verse places Hatthipāla one segment before the Pāli name.

hemaka.notes: The citation list places Hemaka among Bāvarī’s pupils in Snp 5.1. The entry’s verses 1084–1087 are his questions and the Buddha’s reply in Snp 5.9.

hemavata.notes: Snp 1.9 names the speaking yakkha and DN 32 lists him beside Sātāgira. The cited DN 20:7.7–8 uses the plural hemavatā for six thousand Himalayan spirits. It does not single out the chief. The recap at Snp 5.19:20.5 also names the Hemavata discourse.

hārika.notes: SN 19.16:1.5 explicitly names Hārika the executioner (hāriko nāma coraghātako). The headless trunk with eyes and mouth on its chest confirms the identity. DPPN calls him a bandit. Sujato calls him Taker, which explains the missing mention. SN 19.14, 19.15 and 19.17 describe other beings.

hārita.notes: Both dictionaries point to the divine Hārita arriving with his following at DN 20:20.12. The verse gives no identification with Vishnu. The fletcher and arrow in Thag 1.29 identify the monk in Hārita 03. Thag 3.15 is the other elder’s poem and has no candidate entry. The packet misses their names in the respective recaps at Thag 1.30:2.6 and 3.16:5.4.

icchānaṅgala.notes: The Vāseṭṭha episode also appears in MN 98 and Snp 3.9. SN 54.11 describes the retreat and AN 5.30, 6.42 and 8.86 describe the noisy visitors. Those accounts need not concern a single stay. SN 54.20:2.1 is a recap.

indaka.notes: SN 10.1 names the yakkha and records his question about growth in the womb. SN 10.2 concerns Sakka and SN 10.3 Sūciloma. SN 10.12:14.1 lists Indaka in the chapter recap.

indakūṭa.notes: SN 10.1:1.2 places Indaka’s haunt on this mountain. SN 10.2 is set on Gijjhakūṭa and SN 10.3 at Gayā.

isidatta.notes: MN 89 and SN 55.6 name the two chamberlains together as isidattapurāṇā, a compound with its own dictionary line. The elder of SN 41.2–3 and Thag 1.120 has no candidate here. AN 6.44:2.2–5 and AN 10.75 call both laymen once-returners and describe Purāṇa as celibate. Check the entry’s commentary-based qualifications on both points. AN 6.119, AN 6.140 and SN 55.5 are adjacent citation targets.

isipatana.notes: SN 56.11 gives Isipatana’s deer park as the setting of the first sermon. DN 16:5.8.5 describes the pilgrimage site by that event. AN 3.14, 3.127, 6.59, SN 12.66, 22.58, 22.89 and 55.52 are page matches adjacent to texts that name Isipatana.

jambudīpa.notes: AN 9.21 compares the inhabitants (jambudīpakā) with the people of Uttarakuru and the gods of Tāvatiṁsa. AN 9.20 and 9.22 are neighboring texts. Snp 3.7:17.4 uses the alternative name Jambusaṇḍa. The packet misses the place name joined to the following word at DN 30:1.21.17 and Thig 16.1:51.2.

jambugāma.notes: The entry’s DN ii.194 reference is unplaced. DN 16:4.5.3–5 explicitly lists Ambagāma, Jambugāma and Bhoganagara in sequence. The proposed location near Campā is conjectural.

jambuka.notes: In Thag 4.5 Jambuka recalls fifty-five years of austerities, eating dung, taking refuge in the Buddha and attaining the three knowledges. The entry tells both stages of that life and cites the Dhammapada commentary for the ascetic’s story. Thag 4.12:5.3 lists him in the recap.

jambukhādaka.notes: SN 38.1 names Sāriputta’s visitor. SN 37.34 precedes their dialogues. SN 44.11:5.2 lists Jambukhādaka’s collection in a recap.

janavasabha.notes: In DN 18:9.6–10.5 Janavasabha gives his name and identifies himself as Bimbisāra. DN 23:35.3 lists the discourse title.

janesabha.notes: DN 20 and DN 32 both list Janesabha beside Nala. The proposed identification with Janavasabha of DN 18 remains conjectural.

jantu.notes: Jantu addresses the monks in SN 2.25. The god who speaks in SN 2.26 is Rohitassa.

jantugāma.notes: AN 9.3 and Ud 4.1 both recount Meghiya’s almsround in this village. AN 9.2 is the preceding discourse.

jatukaṇṇī.notes: The entry’s verses 1096–1100 belong to Snp 5.12, where Jatukaṇṇī questions the Buddha. The packet quotes his name at 1.2 and misses the Buddha’s address to him at 3.2 (jatukaṇṇīti).

jayasena.notes: MN 125 names Prince Jayasena with the novice Aciravata. MN 126 names him with Bhūmija (spelled Bhūmiya in the entry) and records the prince serving him from his own dish. MN 124 concerns Bākula.

jaṭābhāradvāja.notes: The question about the tangle identifies Jaṭā Bhāradvāja in SN 7.6. SN 7.5 names Ahiṁsaka Bhāradvāja and SN 7.7 names Suddhika Bhāradvāja.

jenta.notes: Verse 111 is attributed to Jenta. Thag 6.9 names the chaplain’s son in its title and attribution, and he recalls his pride of birth. The packet misses their respective recap mentions at Thag 1.120:2.1 and 6.14:7.6. Thig 2.2 names the nun Jentā. SN 7.15 names the brahmin Mānatthaddha, whose identity with the chaplain’s son DPPN only suggests. SN 7.14 concerns a father turned out by his sons.
